extracted.intended_audience: readers, poets, and students of literature / literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for what makes a true poet and a true poem, as articulated in Ralph Waldo Emerson's essay 'The Poet.' Covers originality, imagination, naming, symbolism, expression, moral/spiritual depth, and the poet's relation to nature and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as representative / completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet stands among partial men for the complete man; he is representative of man and apprises us of the common wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'The breadth of the problem is great, for the poet is representative. He stands among partial men for the complete man.' The poet should manifest a largeness of reception and impartation that makes him 'more himself' and thereby more representative to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original announcement (novelty of vision)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet 'announces that which no man foretold' — the sign and credentials of the true poet is originality in revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasized repeatedly: the poet 'is the true and only doctor; he knows and tells; he is the only teller of news.' Talent without this prophetic novelty is only contemporary or ornamental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought prior to form / metre-making argument
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem is made by a 'metre-making argument' — a thought so passionate and alive that it has an architecture of its own; thought (new experience) must precede and create form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contra mere polish: 'it is not metres, but a metre-making argument that makes a poem.' The poet must bring a new, whole experience which gives rise organically to form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of perception / perceiving spiritual meaning in the material
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet perceives the instant dependence of form upon soul and explores multiple meanings of sensuous facts; he sees material phenomena as manifestations of the ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson critiques superficial taste and praises minds that 'explore the double meaning, or ... much more manifold meaning, of every sensuous fact.' Poetic insight links material and spiritual layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as the sayer / namer / language-maker
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is the 'sayer' and 'namer' — he makes language and gives things their own names by coming one step nearer to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'By virtue of this science the poet is the Namer or Language-maker... The poets made all the words.' Apt, revelatory naming that rejoices the intellect is a core criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to receive and impart (balance of powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is the person in whom powers are in balance — who both receives (sees) and imparts (expresses) readily and adequately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'The poet is the person in whom these powers are in balance, the man without impediment, who sees and handles that which others dream of.' The criterion includes fluency of expression so impressions translate into speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal intelligibility / durability
rubrics_metrics.description: When the poet speaks adequately his speech becomes 'universally intelligible' and his phrase will be the fittest and most musical and endure — poems that ascend to their nature endure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'his words are universally intelligible as the plants and animals.' Works that truly enact imaginative truth will 'take care of their own immortality.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of nature as symbol / symbolic imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature is offered as a picture-language; the poet uses natural things as symbols and reads the universe as a temple of emblems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'Nature offers all her creatures to him as a picture-language.' The poet must see and deploy the symbolic power of ordinary things to convey higher meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluidity of symbols (avoid frozen mysticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols must not be nailed to a single private meaning; imagination flows and symbols are fluxional, not fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with mystic mistake: 'the difference betwixt the poet and the mystic, that the last nails a symbol to one sense.' Good poetic symbolism remains flexible and transferable among readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to sanctify or incorporate the new and mechanical
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet re-attaches artificial or new facts (factory-village, railway) to the great Order of nature, making them part of poetic vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson argues that 'the poet sees them fall within the great Order not less than the beehive or the spider's geometrical web' — criterion: poet's capacity to assimilate novel modern facts into a sustaining poetic whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/ethical sympathy (beauty rests on goodness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of beauty should be sympathetic or proper only to the good; the beautiful rests on foundations of the necessary and the moral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'The beautiful rests on the foundations of the necessary. The soul makes the body...' Poetic perception is allied to moral depth and goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humble and mean types as potent symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Small and mean things serve as effective, pungent, and lasting symbols; the poorer the type the more poignant its emblematic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: barberies like 'the poorest experience is rich enough' and 'the meaner the type ... the more pungent it is.' Poetic economy and simplicity are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific/synthetical knowledge of nature (poet as true scientist of signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet understands astronomy, chemistry, vegetation, etc., not as mere facts but as signs — employing natural facts as symbols of human and cosmic life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'The poet alone knows astronomy, chemistry, vegetation and animation, for he ... employs them as signs.' Criterion: synthetic, symbolic science rather than narrow empirical detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veracity of report (genuineness vs. mere talent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius 'realizes and adds' — the value of genius lies in the veracity of its report; mere talent may 'frolic and juggle' but not truly reveal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson recounts eagerness at the advent of a true poet whose report is believable and revolutionary; authenticity of the poet's inner discovery is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emancipatory effect on readers
rubrics_metrics.description: A great imaginative work liberates and exhilarates readers by revealing new relations and opening 'another world' ; poetry's worth includes its power to free the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'The poets are thus liberating gods.' Criterion: the poem's capacity to emancipate thought and feeling in its audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receptivity through abandonment / surrender to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet unlocks himself to the 'public power' by abandonment to the nature of things; this receptive surrender produces the heightened energy of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson describes 'an intellect doubled on itself' achieved by 'abandonment to the nature of things' and compares it to trusting an animal's instinct — a readiness to be carried into universal life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of artificial stimulants for true inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: True inspiration comes to the 'pure and simple soul in a clean and chaste body'; narcotics and artificial excitants produce counterfeit excitement not genuine poetic vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson notes the use of wine, opium, etc., as 'auxiliaries' but warns: 'The sublime vision comes to the pure and simple soul ... That is not an inspiration, which we owe to narcotics.' Lifestyle and bodily purity are presented as conditions for true poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality and fittest phrase as evidence of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The truest word will be the fittest and most musical; poetic diction should possess a natural music that matches the truth it announces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emerson: 'It is the truest word ever spoken, and the phrase will be the fittest, most musical, and the unerring voice of the world for that time.' Diction must serve revelation, not ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence through imaginative truth (poems as immortal progeny)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the poet detaches his poems they become 'fearless, sleepless, deathless progeny' that survive beyond accidents of time; imaginative truth confers immortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor of poems as offspring with wings: 'These wings are the beauty of the poet's soul ... The melodies of the poet ascend and leap and pierce into the deeps of infinite time.' Durability of effect is a mark of success.
